```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")

library(tidyverse)

```

This page summarises what we covered in the first hour of Session 4.
Use it for revision; the full activities were worked through in class.

**Progression:** estimate ÷ SE = t → read the p-value from the
t-distribution, allowing for sample size → the coefficients of a linear
model as a line.

## Strength of evidence as a ratio {#sec-s4-ratio}

We compared six scenarios, each a difference between two group means
with its standard error:

| Scenario   | A   | B   | C   | D   | E   | F   |
|------------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| Difference | 2.0 | 2.0 | 2.0 | 0.5 | 2.0 | 5.0 |
| SE         | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |

The same difference is more convincing when it is measured more
precisely (A, B, C), and a larger difference is more convincing at the
same precision (D, E, F). Scenarios B and E look equally convincing.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
The strength of evidence depends on the size of the estimate compared
with its standard error. This ratio is the **t-statistic**:
t = estimate / standard error. A large t, positive or negative, means
the estimate is many standard errors away from zero. Because the units
cancel, t means the same thing whatever the units of the data.
:::

The study in the Session 3 exit question (coefficient 1.2, SE 0.5) has
t = 2.4. Darwin's mean paired difference (2.62 inches, SE 1.22) has
t ≈ 2.15.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** In Scenario C, the t-statistic is
`r fitb(1)`.

`r hide("Explanation")`
t = 2.0 / 2.0 = 1.0. Compare this with Scenario A, where t = 4.0.
The ratio, not the estimate alone, determines the evidence.
`r unhide()`
:::

## The shortcut curve {#sec-s4-curve}

In Session 3 we built a null distribution by flipping the signs of
Darwin's differences, and each run of shuffles gave a slightly
different p-value. A computer can instead list every possible sign
pattern: with 15 pairs there are 32 768, but with 30 pairs there would
be over a billion. @fig-s4-perm-vs-t shows t for all 32 768 patterns,
with the t-distribution for 14 degrees of freedom drawn over it. The
curve comes from a formula: nobody had to shuffle anything to draw it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-s4-perm-vs-t
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Bars: the null distribution of t from all 32 768 sign patterns of Darwin's differences. Line: the t-distribution with 14 degrees of freedom. Dashed lines: Darwin's t and its mirror."

darwin_d <- c(6.125, -8.375, 1, 2, 0.75, 2.875, 3.5, 5.125,
              1.75, 3.625, 7, 3, 9.375, 7.5, -6)
n <- length(darwin_d)
t_obs <- mean(darwin_d) / (sd(darwin_d) / sqrt(n))

sign_patterns <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(c(-1, 1)), n)))

perm_t <- apply(sign_patterns, 1, function(s) {
  x <- darwin_d * s
  mean(x) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n))
})

tibble(t = perm_t) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.25,
                 boundary = 0, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = n - 1), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_obs, t_obs), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "t calculated for each sign pattern (if H0 is true)",
       y = "Density")
```

| Method                                | What you need                             | Two-sided p-value |
|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| List all 32 768 sign patterns         | All 15 differences and a lot of computing | 0.053             |
| Read the area from the t-distribution | Just t = 2.15 and 14 degrees of freedom   | 0.0497            |

The curve follows the bars closely, so the two p-values are almost the
same. In Session 3, `t.test()` gave p = 0.025: that was one-sided,
counting one tail only. Counting both tails doubles it, to about 0.050.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
If the null hypothesis is true and the data are roughly normal, the
null distribution of t follows a known curve: the **t-distribution**.
So instead of building the null distribution, you calculate t and read
the p-value from the curve. This is the shortcut that `t.test()` and
`lm()` use. With small samples that are skewed or contain extreme
values, the curve can be a poor match, so plot your data before relying
on the shortcut.
:::

## Same t, different sample size {#sec-s4-df}

The shape of the t-distribution depends on the **degrees of freedom**
(df); for paired differences, df is the number of pairs minus one. The
95% multiplier is the value t must exceed for a two-sided p-value below
0.05:

| df             | 3    | 4    | 14   | 30   | 100  | Very large |
|----------------|------|------|------|------|------|------------|
| 95% multiplier | 3.18 | 2.78 | 2.14 | 2.04 | 1.98 | 1.96       |

Three studies all found a mean paired difference of 2.62 with an SE of
1.22, so all three had t = 2.15. They differed only in the number of
pairs:

| Study | Pairs | df  | 95% multiplier | t = 2.15 bigger? | p-value |
|-------|-------|-----|----------------|------------------|---------|
| X     | 5     | 4   | 2.78           | No               | 0.098   |
| Y     | 15    | 14  | 2.14           | Only just        | 0.050   |
| Z     | 101   | 100 | 1.98           | Yes              | 0.034   |

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
The t-distribution allows for sample size. With few observations, the
SE is itself estimated unreliably, so the t-distribution has heavier
tails and t must clear a higher bar. The degrees of freedom set that
bar. The same t can give p below 0.05 in a large study and not in a
small one. As the sample grows, the multiplier approaches 1.96, the
value used for confidence intervals in Session 2.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A study of 4 pairs finds t = 2.5. Is its
two-sided p-value below 0.05?

`r mcq(c("Yes", answer = "No"))`

`r hide("Explanation")`
With 4 pairs, df = 3 and the 95% multiplier is 3.18. A t of 2.5 does
not clear it, so p is above 0.05. With 31 pairs (df = 30, multiplier
2.04), the same t would give p below 0.05.
`r unhide()`
:::

## From two means to a line {#sec-s4-line}

To draw a comparison of two group means as a line, each group is given
a number: Cross is x = 0 and Self is x = 1. Darwin's mean heights were
20.19 inches (Cross) and 17.58 inches (Self).

```{r}
#| label: fig-s4-line
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Darwin's two group means, coded x = 0 (Cross) and x = 1 (Self), joined by a straight line. The intercept is the Cross mean; the slope is the difference between the means."

tibble(x = c(0, 1), height = c(20.19, 17.58)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = height)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Cross\n(x = 0)", "Self\n(x = 1)"),
                     limits = c(-0.5, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "Fertilisation type", y = "Mean height (inches)")
```

The line has an intercept of 20.19 (its height at x = 0) and a slope of
−2.62 (the change from x = 0 to x = 1). These are exactly the two
estimates `lm(height ~ type)` reports in hour 2: `(Intercept)` = 20.19
and `typeSelf` = −2.62.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
Giving the groups the numbers 0 and 1 turns a comparison of two means
into a straight line. The intercept is the mean of the group coded 0,
the **reference level**. The slope is the difference between the two
means. These are the two coefficients a linear model reports. The
x-axis is a label, not a measurement: the line does not mean that
height changes gradually between the groups.
:::

We then returned to the Session 3 exit question by adding an invented
third treatment with a mean height of 19.00 inches. The model compares
every treatment with the reference level, so it needs two differences:
Self − Cross = −2.62 and Third − Cross = −1.19.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
Each treatment is measured as its own step from the reference level. A
model with three groups therefore reports an intercept and two
coefficients, one for each treatment that is not the reference. A
single difference of means is no longer enough. Models like this are
fitted in Session 6.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A model compares four groups. How many
coefficients does it report in addition to the intercept?
`r fitb(3)`
:::

> p-value below 0.05? Explain why.
